entries.8c0098b3b52ec81a69eef093f3f9b8e2f71f5d8f: <div sID="gen2158" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="35" osisID="Exod.35" sID="Exod.35"/> <div eID="gen2158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2159" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2160" type="x-p"/> What should have been said and done upon Moses' coming down the first time from the mount, if the golden calf had not broken the measures and put all into disorder, now at last, when with great difficulty reconciliation was made, begins to be said and done; and that great affair of the setting up of God's worship is put into its former channel again, and goes on now without interruption. I. Moses gives Israel those instructions, received from God, which required immediate observance. 1. Concerning the sabbath, <reference osisRef="Exod.35.1-Exod.35.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. 2. Concerning the contribution that was to be made for the erecting of the tabernacle, <reference osisRef="Exod.35.4-Exod.35.9">ver. 4-9</reference>. 3. Concerning the framing of the tabernacle and the utensils of it, <reference osisRef="Exod.35.10-Exod.35.19">ver. 10-19</reference>. II. The people bring in their contributions, <reference osisRef="Exod.35.20-Exod.35.29">ver. 20-29</reference>. III. The head-workmen are nominated, <reference osisRef="Exod.35.30-Exod.35.35">ver. 30</reference>, &c.
entries.8a756115d347009ee3271d6a7318c033c29ed66e: <div eID="gen2160" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2159" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Orders Concerning the Tabernacle. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen2161" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And Moses gathered all the congregation of the children of Israel together, and said unto them, These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the words which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath commanded, that <hi type="italic">ye</hi> should do them. <hi type="super">2</hi> Six days shall work be done, but on the seventh day there shall be to you an holy day, a sabbath of rest to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : whosoever doeth work therein shall be put to death. <hi type="super">3</hi> Ye shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations upon the sabbath day. <hi type="super">4</hi> And Moses spake unto all the congregation of the children of Israel, saying, This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the thing which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded, saying, <hi type="super">5</hi> Take ye from among you an offering unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : whosoever <hi type="italic">is</hi> of a willing heart, let him bring it, an offering of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; gold, and silver, and brass, <hi type="super">6</hi> And blue, and purple, and scarlet, and fine linen, and goats' <hi type="italic">hair,</hi> <hi type="super">7</hi> And rams' skins dyed red, and badgers' skins, and shittim wood, <hi type="super">8</hi> And oil for the light, and spices for anointing oil, and for the sweet incense, <hi type="super">9</hi> And onyx stones, and stones to be set for the ephod, and for the breastplate. <hi type="super">10</hi> And every wise hearted among you shall come, and make all that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath commanded; <hi type="super">11</hi> The tabernacle, his tent, and his covering, his taches, and his boards, his bars, his pillars, and his sockets, <hi type="super">12</hi> The ark, and the staves thereof, <hi type="italic">with</hi> the mercy seat, and the vail of the covering, <hi type="super">13</hi> The table, and his staves, and all his vessels, and the showbread, <hi type="super">14</hi> The candlestick also for the light, and his furniture, and his lamps, with the oil for the light, <hi type="super">15</hi> And the incense altar, and his staves, and the anointing oil, and the sweet incense, and the hanging for the door at the entering in of the tabernacle, <hi type="super">16</hi> The altar of burnt offering, with his brazen grate, his staves, and all his vessels, the laver and his foot, <hi type="super">17</hi> The hangings of the court, his pillars, and their sockets, and the hanging for the door of the court, <hi type="super">18</hi> The pins of the tabernacle, and the pins of the court, and their cords, <hi type="super">19</hi> The cloths of service, to do service in the holy <hi type="italic">place,</hi> the holy garments for Aaron the priest, and the garments of his sons, to minister in the priest's office. <div eID="gen2161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2162" type="x-p"/> It was said in general (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.32">ch. xxxiv. 32</reference>), <hi type="italic">Moses gave them in commandment all that the Lord has spoken with him.</hi> But, the erecting and furnishing of the tabernacle being the work to which they were now immediately to apply themselves, there is particular mention of the orders given concerning it. <div eID="gen2162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2163" type="x-p"/> I. All the congregation is summoned to attend (<reference osisRef="Exod.35.1">v. 1</reference>); that is, the heads and rulers of the congregation, the representatives of the several tribes, who must receive instructions from Moses as he had received them from the Lord, and must communicate them to the people. Thus John, being commanded to write to the seven churches what had been revealed to him, writes it to the angels, or ministers, of the churches. <div eID="gen2163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2164" type="x-p"/> II. Moses gave them in charge all that (and that only) which God had commanded him; thus he approved himself faithful both to God and Israel, between whom he was a messenger or mediator. If he had added, altered, or diminished, he would have been false to both. But, both sides having reposed a trust in him, he was true to the trust; yet he was faithful as a servant only, but <hi type="italic">Christ as a Son,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.3.5-Heb.3.6">Heb. iii. 5, 6</reference>. <div eID="gen2164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2165" type="x-p"/> III. He begins with the law of the sabbath, because that was much insisted on in the instructions he had received (<reference osisRef="Exod.35.2-Exod.35.3">v. 2, 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Six days shall work be done,</hi> work for the tabernacle, the work of the day that was now to be done in its day; and they had little else to do here in the wilderness, where they had neither husbandry nor merchandise, neither food to get nor clothes to make: <hi type="italic">but on the seventh day</hi> you must not strike a stroke, no, not at the tabernacle-work; the honour of the sabbath was above that of the sanctuary, more ancient and more lasting; that must be to you a holy day, devoted to God, and not be spent in common business. It is a sabbath of rest. It is a <hi type="italic">sabbath of sabbaths</hi> (so some read it), more honourable and excellent than any of the other feasts, and should survive them all. A <hi type="italic">sabbath of sabbatism,</hi> so others read it, being typical of that sabbatism or rest, both spiritual and eternal, which <hi type="italic">remains for the people of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.4.9">Heb. iv. 9</reference>. It is a sabbath of rest, that is, in which a rest from all worldly labour must be very carefully and strictly observed. It is a sabbath and a little sabbath, so some of the Jews would have it read; not only observing the whole day as a sabbath, but an hour before the beginning of it, and an hour after the ending of it, which they throw in over and above out of their own time, and call <hi type="italic">a little sabbath,</hi> to show how glad they are of the approach of the sabbath and how loth to part with it. It is a sabbath of rest, but it is rest to the Lord, to whose honour it must be devoted. A penalty is here annexed to the breach of it: <hi type="italic">Whosoever doeth work therein shall be put to death.</hi> Also a particular prohibition of kindling fires on the sabbath day for any servile work, as smith's work, or plumbers, &c. <div eID="gen2165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2166" type="x-p"/> IV. He orders preparation to be made for the setting up of the tabernacle. Two things were to be done:— <div eID="gen2166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2167" type="x-p"/> 1. All that were able must contribute: <hi type="italic">Take you from among you an offering,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.35.5">v. 5</reference>. The tabernacle was to be dedicated to the honour of God, and used in his service; and therefore what was brought for the setting up and furnishing of that was <hi type="italic">an offering to the Lord.</hi> Our goodness extends not to God, but what is laid out for the support of his kingdom and interest among men he is pleased to accept as an offering to himself; and he requires such acknowledgements of our receiving our all from him and such instances of our dedicating our all to him. The rule is, <hi type="italic">Whosoever is of a willing heart let him bring.</hi> It was not to be a tax imposed upon them, but a benevolence or voluntary contribution, to intimate to us, (1.) That God has not made our yoke heavy. He is a prince that does not burden his subjects with taxes, nor <hi type="italic">make them to serve with an offering,</hi> but <hi type="italic">draws with the cords of a man,</hi> and leaves it to ourselves to <hi type="italic">judge what is right;</hi> his is a government that there is no cause to complain of, for he does not rule with rigour. (2.) That God loves a cheerful giver, and is best pleased with the free-will offering. Those services are acceptable to him that come from the willing heart of a willing people, <reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">Ps. cx. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen2167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2168" type="x-p"/> 2. All that were skilful must work: <hi type="italic">Every wise-hearted among you shall come, and make,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.35.10">v. 10</reference>. See how God dispenses his gifts variously; and, <hi type="italic">as every man hath received the gift, so he must minister,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.10">1 Pet. iv. 10</reference>. Those that were rich must bring in materials to work on; those that were ingenious must serve the tabernacle with their ingenuity; as they needed one another, so the tabernacle needed them both, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.7-1Cor.12.21">1 Cor. xii. 7-21</reference>. The work was likely to go on when some helped with their purses, others with their hands, and both with a willing heart. Moses, as he had told them what must be given (<reference osisRef="Exod.35.5-Exod.35.9">v. 5-9</reference>), so he gives them the general heads of what must be made (<reference osisRef="Exod.35.11-Exod.35.19">v. 11-19</reference>), that, seeing how much work was before them, they might apply themselves to it the more vigorously, and every hand might be busy; and it gave them such an idea of the fabric designed that they could not but long to see it finished.
entries.2669c73cc643504948afaf30b34eec8ea38eb4b7: <div eID="gen2168" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Contributions for the Tabernacle. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen2169" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> And all the congregation of the children of Israel departed from the presence of Moses. <hi type="super">21</hi> And they came, every one whose heart stirred him up, and every one whom his spirit made willing, <hi type="italic">and</hi> they brought the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's offering to the work of the tabernacle of the congregation, and for all his service, and for the holy garments. <hi type="super">22</hi> And they came, both men and women, as many as were willing hearted, <hi type="italic">and</hi> brought bracelets, and earrings, and rings, and tablets, all jewels of gold: and every man that offered <hi type="italic">offered</hi> an offering of gold unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">23</hi> And every man, with whom was found blue, and purple, and scarlet, and fine linen, and goats' <hi type="italic">hair,</hi> and red skins of rams, and badgers' skins, brought <hi type="italic">them.</hi> <hi type="super">24</hi> Every one that did offer an offering of silver and brass brought the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's offering: and every man, with whom was found shittim wood for any work of the service, brought <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">25</hi> And all the women that were wise hearted did spin with their hands, and brought that which they had spun, <hi type="italic">both</hi> of blue, and of purple, <hi type="italic">and</hi> of scarlet, and of fine linen. <hi type="super">26</hi> And all the women whose heart stirred them up in wisdom spun goats' <hi type="italic">hair.</hi> <hi type="super">27</hi> And the rulers brought onyx stones, and stones to be set, for the ephod, and for the breastplate; <hi type="super">28</hi> And spice, and oil for the light, and for the anointing oil, and for the sweet incense. 29 The children of Israel brought a willing offering unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , every man and woman, whose heart made them willing to bring for all manner of work, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had commanded to be made by the hand of Moses. <div eID="gen2169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2170" type="x-p"/> Moses having made known to them the will of God, they went home and immediately put in practice what they had heard, <reference osisRef="Exod.35.20">v. 20</reference>. O that every congregation would thus depart from the hearing of the word of God, with a full resolution to be <hi type="italic">doers of the same!</hi> Observe here, <div eID="gen2170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2171" type="x-p"/> I. The offerings that were brought for the service of the tabernacle (<reference osisRef="Exod.35.21">v. 21</reference>, &c.), concerning which many things may be noted. 1. It is intimated that they brought their offerings immediately; they departed to their tents immediately to fetch their offering, and did not desire time to consider of it, lest their zeal should be cooled by delays. What duty God convinces us of, and calls us to, we should set about speedily. No season will be more convenient than the present season. 2. It is said that <hi type="italic">their spirits made them willing</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.35.21">v. 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">and their hearts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.35.29">v. 29</reference>. What they did they did cheerfully, and from a good principle. They were willing, and it was not any external inducement that made them so, but their spirits. It was from a principle of love to God and his service, a desire of his presence with them in his ordinances, gratitude for the great things he had done for them, faith in his promise of what he would further do (or, at least, from the present consideration of these things), that they were willing to offer. What we give and do for God is then acceptable when it comes from a good principle in the heart and spirit. 3. When it is said that as many as were willing-hearted brought their offerings (<reference osisRef="Exod.35.22">v. 22</reference>), it should seem as if there were some who were not, who loved their gold better than their God, and would not part with it, no, not for the service of the tabernacle. Such there are, who will be called Israelites, and yet will not be moved by the equity of the thing, God's expectations from them, and the good examples of those about them, to part with any thing for the interests of God's kingdom: they are for the true religion, provided it be cheap and will cost them nothing. 4. The offerings were of divers kinds, according as they had; those that had gold and precious stones brought them, not thinking any thing too good and too rich to part with for the honour of God. Those that had not precious stones to bring brought goats' hair, and rams' skins. If we cannot do as much as others for God, we must not therefore sit still and do nothing: if the meaner offerings which are according to our ability gain us not such a reputation among men, yet they shall not fail of acceptance with God, who requires <hi type="italic">according to what a man hath, and not according to what he hath not,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.12">2 Cor. viii. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.23">2 Kings v. 23</reference>. Two mites from a pauper were more pleasing than so many talents from a Dives. God has an eye to the heart of the giver more than to the value of the gift. 5. Many of the things they offered were their ornaments, bracelets and rings, and tablets or lockets (<reference osisRef="Exod.35.22">v. 22</reference>); and even the women parted with these. <hi type="italic">Can a maid forget her ornaments?</hi> Thus far they forgot them that they preferred the beautifying of the sanctuary before their own adorning. Let this teach us, in general, to part with that for God, when he calls for it, which is very dear to us, which we value, and value ourselves by; and particularly to lay aside our ornaments, and deny ourselves in them, when either they occasion offence to others or feed our own pride. If we think those gospel rules concerning our clothing too strict (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.9-1Tim.2.10">1 Tim. ii. 9, 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.3-1Pet.3.4">1 Pet. iii. 3, 4</reference>), I fear we should scarcely have done as these Israelites did. If they thought their ornaments well bestowed upon the tabernacle, shall not we think the want of ornaments well made up by the graces of the Spirit? <reference osisRef="Prov.1.9">Prov. i. 9</reference>. 6. These rich things that they offered, we may suppose, were mostly the spoils of the Egyptians; for the Israelites in Egypt were kept poor, till they borrowed at parting. And we may suppose the rulers had better things (<reference osisRef="Exod.35.27">v. 27</reference>), because, having more influence among the Egyptians, they borrowed larger sums. Who would have thought that ever the wealth of Egypt should have been so well employed? but thus God has often made <hi type="italic">the earth to help the woman,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.12.16">Rev. xii. 16</reference>. It was by a special providence and promise of God that the Israelites got all that spoil, and therefore it was highly fit that they should devote a part of it to the service of that God to whom they owed it all. Let every man give <hi type="italic">according as God hath prospered him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.2">1 Cor. xvi. 2</reference>. Extraordinary successes should be acknowledged by extraordinary offerings. Apply it to human learning, arts and sciences, which are borrowed, as it were, from the Egyptians. Those that are enriched with these must devote them to the service of God and his tabernacle: they may be used as helps to understand the scriptures, as ornaments or handmaids to divinity. But then great care must be taken that Egypt's gods mingle not with Egypt's gold. Moses, though learned in all the learning of the Egyptians, did not therefore pretend, in the least instance, to correct the pattern shown him in the mount. The furnishing of the tabernacle with the riches of Egypt was perhaps a good omen to the Gentiles, who, in the fulness of time, should be brought into the gospel tabernacle, and their silver and their gold with them (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.9">Isa. lx. 9</reference>), and it should be said, <hi type="italic">Blessed be Egypt my people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.19.25">Isa. xix. 25</reference>. 7. We may suppose that the remembrance of the offerings made for the golden calf made them the more forward in these offerings. Those that had then parted with their ear-rings would not testify their repentance by giving the rest of their jewels to the service of God: godly sorrow worketh such a revenge, <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.11">2 Cor. vii. 11</reference>. And those that had kept themselves pure from that idolatry yet argued with themselves, "Were they so forward in contributing to an idol, and shall we be backward or sneaking in our offerings to the Lord?" Thus some good was brought even out of that evil. <div eID="gen2171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2172" type="x-p"/> II. The work that was done for the service of the tabernacle (<reference osisRef="Exod.35.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">The women did spin with their hands.</hi> Some spun fine work, of blue and purple; others coarse work, of goats' hair, and yet theirs also is said to be done in wisdom, <reference osisRef="Exod.35.26">v. 26</reference>. As it is not only rich gifts, so it is not only fine work that God accepts. Notice is here taken of the good women's work for God, as well as of Bezaleel's and Aholiab's. The meanest hand for the honour of God, shall have an honourable recompence. Mary's anointing of Christ's head shall be told for a memorial (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.13">Matt. xxvi. 13</reference>); and a record is kept of the women that laboured in the gospel tabernacle (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.3">Phil. iv. 3</reference>), and were helpers to Paul in Christ Jesus, <reference osisRef="Rom.16.3">Rom. xvi. 3</reference>. It is part of the character of the virtuous woman that she layeth <hi type="italic">her hands to the spindle,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.31.19">Prov. xxxi. 19</reference>. This employment was here turned to a pious use, as it may be still (though we have no hangings to make for the tabernacle) by the imitation of the charity of Dorcas, who made coats and garments for poor widows, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.39">Acts ix. 39</reference>. Even those that are not in a capacity to give in charity may yet work in charity; and thus the poor may relieve the poor, and those that have nothing but their limbs and senses may be very charitable in the labour of love.
entries.748d095e26545f29f93540d4e4cc9c0a43f496ec: <div eID="gen2172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2173" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">30</hi> And Moses said unto the children of Israel, See, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath called by name Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah; 31 And he hath filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship; <hi type="super">32</hi> And to devise curious works, to work in gold, and in silver, and in brass, <hi type="super">33</hi> And in the cutting of stones, to set <hi type="italic">them,</hi> and in carving of wood, to make any manner of cunning work. <hi type="super">34</hi> And he hath put in his heart that he may teach, <hi type="italic">both</hi> he, and Aholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of <reference osisRef="Dan.35">Dan. 35</reference> Them hath he filled with wisdom of heart, to work all manner of work, of the engraver, and of the cunning workman, and of the embroiderer, in blue, and in purple, in scarlet, and in fine linen, and of the weaver, <hi type="italic">even</hi> of them that do any work, and of those that devise cunning work. <div eID="gen2173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2174" type="x-p"/> Here is the divine appointment of the master-workmen, that there might be no strife for the office, and that all who were employed in the work might take direction from, and give account to, these general inspectors; for God is the God of order and not of confusion. Observe, 1. Those whom God called by name to this service he <hi type="italic">filled with the Spirit of God,</hi> to qualify them for it, <reference osisRef="Exod.35.30-Exod.35.31">v. 30, 31</reference>. Skill in secular employments is God's gift, and comes from above, <reference osisRef="Jas.1.17">Jam. i. 17</reference>. From him the faculty is, and the improvement of it. To his honour therefore all knowledge must be devoted, and we must study how to serve him with it. The work was extraordinary which Bezaleel was designed for, and therefore he was qualified in an extraordinary manner for it; thus when the apostles were appointed to be master-builders in setting up the gospel tabernacle they were <hi type="italic">filled with the Spirit of God in wisdom and understanding.</hi> 2. The were appointed, not only to devise, but to work (<reference osisRef="Exod.35.32">v. 32</reference>), <hi type="italic">to work all manner of work,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.35.35">v. 35</reference>. Those of eminent gifts, that are capable of directing others, must not think that these will excuse them in idleness. Many are ingenious enough in cutting out work for other people, and can tell what this man and that man should do, but the burdens they bind on others they themselves <hi type="italic">will not touch with one of their fingers.</hi> These will fall under the character of slothful servants. 3. They were not only to devise and work themselves, but they were to teach others, <reference osisRef="Exod.35.34">v. 34</reference>. Not only had Bezaleel power to command, but he was to take pains to instruct. Those that rule should teach; and those to whom God had given knowledge should be willing to communicate it for the benefit of others, not coveting to monopolize it.  <chapter eID="Exod.35"/> <div eID="gen2174" type="x-p"/>

entries.0967217ec253d481ad1178fb971eeb3b85c14463: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv945"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 35</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Exod.35.1-Exod.35.35">Ex 35:1-35</reference>. Contributions to the Tabernacle.</title> <div sID="gen1309" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv945"/><hi type="bold">1. Moses gathered all the congregation of the children of Israel, &c.--</hi>On the occasion referred to in the opening of this chapter, the Israelites were specially reminded of the design to erect a magnificent tabernacle for the regular worship of God, as well as of the leading articles that were required to furnish that sacred edifice [Ex 35:11-19]. (See on <reference osisRef="Exod.25.1-Exod.25.40">Ex 25:1-40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.27.1-Exod.27.21">Ex 27:1-21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.30.1-Exod.31.18">Ex 30:1-31:18</reference>). <div eID="gen1309" type="x-p"/>
entries.2c2e1533633cc2bb0412402000a382ad53343cc6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv946"/><div sID="gen1310" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv946"/><hi type="bold">20-21. all the congregation of Israel departed from the presence of Moses--</hi>No exciting harangues were made, nor had the people Bibles at home in which they could compare the requirements of their leader and see if these things were so. But they had no doubt as to his bearing to them the will of God, and they were impressed with so strong a sense of its being their duty, that they made a spontaneous offer of the best and most valuable treasures they possessed. <div eID="gen1310" type="x-p"/>
entries.0d0f56299109e4807c0f0bae065bf8e451c7a8c9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv948"/><div sID="gen1313" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv948"/><hi type="bold">22. they came, both men and women, &c.--</hi>literally, "the men over and above the women"; a phraseology which implies that the women acted a prominent part, presented their offerings first, and then were followed by as many of their male companions as were similarly disposed.<div eID="gen1313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1314" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brought bracelets, &c.--</hi>There was in that early age no money in the form of coins or bullion. What money passed current with the merchant consisted of rings which were weighed, and principally of ornaments for personal decoration. Astonishment at the abundance of their ornaments is at an end when we learn that costly and elegant ornaments abounded in proportion as clothing was simple and scarce among the Egyptians, and some, entirely divested of clothing, yet wore rich necklaces [Hengstenberg]. Among people with Oriental sentiments and tastes, scarcely any stronger proof could have been given of the power of religion than their willingness not only to lay aside, but to devote those much-valued trinkets to the house of God; and thus all, like the Eastern sages, laid the best they had at the service of God. <div eID="gen1314" type="x-p"/>
entries.9c30ce661afecadb4104d06bf94dae57f78f74ba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv949"/><div sID="gen1315" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv949"/><hi type="bold">30. See, the Lord hath called by name Bezaleel, the son of Uri, &c.--</hi>Moses had made this communication before [see <reference osisRef="Exod.31.2-Exod.31.5">Ex 31:2-5</reference>; also see on Ex 31:2]. But now that the collection had been made, the materials were contributed, and the operations of building about to be commenced, it was with the greatest propriety he reminded the people that the individuals entrusted with the application of their gold and silver had been nominated to the work by authority to which all would bow. <div eID="gen1315" type="x-p"/>
entries.e5ef355866d10dc089764bc1bcc34367c392abe5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv950"/><div sID="gen1316" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv950"/><hi type="bold">35. Them hath he filled with wisdom of heart--</hi>A statement which not only testifies that skill in art and science is a direct gift from God, but that weaving was especially the business of men in Egypt (see <reference osisRef="Exod.38.22">Ex 38:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.39.22">39:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.39.27">27</reference>). And in perfect harmony with the testimony of the monuments is the account given by Moses to the artists who were divinely taught the arts necessary for the embellishment of the tabernacle. Others, whose limited means did not admit of these expensive contributions, offered their gratuitous services in fabricating such articles of tapestry as were needed; arts which the Israelitish females learned as bondwomen, in the houses of Egyptian princes. <chapter eID="Exod.35"/>

entries.aae2e86f9af72185e1eb0a27c47e95b32985b5d9: <div eID="gen4060" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen4061" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4062" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4062" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4061" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4063" type="x-p"/> Moses assembles the congregation to deliver to them the commandments of God, <reference osisRef="Exo.35.1">Exo 35:1</reference>. The women spin, and bring the produce of their skill and industry, <reference osisRef="Exo.35.25">Exo 35:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.35.26">Exo 35:26</reference>. The rulers bring precious stones, etc., <reference osisRef="Exo.35.27">Exo 35:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.35.28">Exo 35:28</reference>. Bezaleel and Aholiab appointed to conduct and superintend all the work of the tabernacle, for which they are qualified by the spirit of wisdom, <reference osisRef="Exo.35.30-Exo.35.35">Exo 35:30-35</reference>. <div eID="gen4063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4064" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen4064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4065" type="x-p"/> And Moses gathered - The principal subjects in this chapter have been already largely considered in the notes on chapters 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, and 31, and to those the reader is particularly desired to refer, together with the parallel texts in the margin.
entries.0f40abe07d55b74a70da4ba0903216b1d8f6f670: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen4065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4066" type="x-p"/> Ye shall kindle no fire - The Jews understand this precept as forbidding the kindling of fire only for the purpose of doing work or dressing victuals; but to give them light and heat, they judge it lawful to light a fire on the Sabbath day, though themselves rarely kindle it-they get Christians to do this work for them.

entries.c0d2395040c76ecf22e8aafdaf35ea2d119d7b71: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen4079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4080" type="x-p"/> Every one whose heart stirred him up - Literally, whose heart was lifted up - whose affections were set on the work, being cordially engaged in the service of God.
entries.626b0d27f632d36c4c213373eb6e4ef6f5f1fa03: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen4080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4081" type="x-p"/> As many as were willing-hearted - For no one was forced to lend his help in this sacred work; all was a free-will offering to the Lord. <div eID="gen4081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4082" type="x-p"/> Bracelets - חח chach, whatever hooks together; ornaments for the wrists, arms, legs, or neck. <div eID="gen4082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4083" type="x-p"/> Ear-rings - נזם nezem, see this explained <reference osisRef="Gen.24.22">Gen 24:22</reference> (note). <div eID="gen4083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4084" type="x-p"/> Rings - טבעת tabbaath, from טבי taba, to penetrate, enter into; probably rings for the fingers. <div eID="gen4084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4085" type="x-p"/> Tablets - כומז cumaz, a word only used here and in <reference osisRef="Num.31.50">Num 31:50</reference>, supposed to be a girdle to support the breasts.
entries.601b49ba743bfbc9fc50c75b65438baa05cf977c: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen4085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4086" type="x-p"/> All the women that were wise-hearted did spin - They had before learned this art, they were wise-hearted; and now they practice it, and God condescends to require and accept their services. In building this house of God, all were ambitious to do something by which they might testify their piety to God, and their love for his worship. The spinning practiced at this time was simple, and required little apparatus. It was the plain distaff or twirling pin, which might be easily made out of any wood they met with in the wilderness.
entries.c54a7241a67e6e91b86861fc37eef3326beb8dc5: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen4086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4087" type="x-p"/> The rulers brought onyx stones - These being persons of consequence, might be naturally expected to furnish the more scarce and costly articles. See how all join in this service! The men worked and brought offerings, the women spun and brought their ornaments, the rulers united with them, and delivered up their jewels! and all the children of Israel brought a willing offering unto the Lord, <reference osisRef="Exo.36.29">Exo 36:29</reference>.
entries.24a42edcd1a632514e3810b477ab2d3e43ee9174: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen4087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4088" type="x-p"/> The Lord hath called by name Bezaleel - See this subject discussed at large in the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.28.3">Exo 28:3</reference> (note), where the subject of superseding the work of the hand by the extra use of machinery is particularly considered. <div eID="gen4088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4089" type="x-p"/> 1. From the nature of the offerings made for the service of the tabernacle, we see of what sort the spoils were which the Israelites brought out of Egypt: gold, silver, brass, blue, purple, scarlet, fine linen, rams' skins dyed red, what we call badgers' skins, oil, spices, incense, onyx stones, and other stones, the names of which are not here mentioned. They must also have brought looms, spinning wheels, instruments for cutting precious stones, anvils, hammers, furnaces, melting-pots, with a vast variety of tools for the different artists employed on the work of the tabernacle, viz., smiths, joiners, carvers, gilders, etc. <div eID="gen4089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4090" type="x-p"/> 2. God could have erected his tabernacle without the help or skill of man; but he condescended to employ him. As all are interested in the worship of God, so all should bear a part in it; here God employs the whole congregation: every male and female, with even their sons and their daughters, and the very ornaments of their persons, are given to raise and adorn the house of God. The women who had not ornaments, and could neither give gold nor silver, could spin goat's hair, and the Lord graciously employs them in this work, and accepts what they can give and what they can do, for they did it with a willing mind; they were wise of heart - had learned a useful business, their hearts were lifted up in the work, <reference osisRef="Exo.36.21">Exo 36:21</reference>, and all felt it a high privilege to be able to put only a nail in the holy place. By the free-will offerings of the people the tabernacle was erected, and all the costly utensils belonging to it provided. This was the primitive mode of providing proper places for Divine worship; and as it was the primitive, so it is the most rational mode. Taxes levied by law for building or repairing churches were not known in the ancient times of religious simplicity. It is an honor to be permitted to do any thing for the support of public worship; and he must have a strange, unfeeling, and ungodly heart, who does not esteem it a high privilege to have a stone of his own laying or procuring in the house of God. How easily might all the buildings necessary for the purpose of public worship be raised, if the money that is spent in needless self-indulgence by ourselves, our sons, and our daughters, were devoted to this purpose! By sacrifices of this kind the house of the Lord would be soon built, and the top-stone brought on with shouting, Grace, grace unto it!  <chapter eID="Exod.35"/> <div eID="gen4090" type="x-p"/>

entries.ac68b8463b01882216fcc6355c5e57a9ee448528: Preliminaries to the Work. - <reference osisRef="Exod.35.1">Ex 35:1</reference>-29. After the restoration of the covenant, Moses announced to the people the divine commands with reference to the holy place of the tabernacle which was to be built. He repeated first of all (<reference osisRef="Exod.35.1-Exod.35.3">Exo 35:1-3</reference>) the law of the Sabbath according to <reference osisRef="Exod.31.13-Exod.31.17">Exo 31:13-17</reference>, and strengthened it by the announcement, that on the Sabbath no fire was to be kindled in their dwelling, because this rule was to be observed even in connection with the work to be done for the tabernacle. (For a fuller comment, see at Exo 20:9.). Then, in accordance with the command of Jehovah, he first of all summoned the whole nation to present freewill-offerings for the holy things to be prepared (<reference osisRef="Exod.35.4">Exo 35:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.35.5">Exo 35:5</reference>), mentioning one by one all the materials that would be required (<reference osisRef="Exod.35.5-Exod.35.9">Exo 35:5-9</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.25.3-Exod.25.7">Exo 25:3-7</reference>); and after that he called upon those who were endowed with understanding to prepare the different articles, as prescribed in ch. 25-30, mentioning these also one by one (<reference osisRef="Exod.35.11-Exod.35.19">Exo 35:11-19</reference>), even down to the pegs of the dwelling and court (<reference osisRef="Exod.27.19">Exo 27:19</reference>), and “their cords,” i.e., the cords required to fasten the tent and the hangings round the court to the pegs that were driven into the ground, which had not been mentioned before, being altogether subordinate things. (On the “cloths of service,” <reference osisRef="Exod.35.19">Exo 35:19</reference>, see at Exo 31:10.) In <reference osisRef="Exod.35.20-Exod.35.29">Exo 35:20-29</reference> we have an account of the fulfilment of this command. The people went from Moses, i.e., from the place where they were assembled round Moses, away to their tents, and willingly offered the things required as a heave-offering for Jehovah; every one “whom his heart lifted up,” i.e., who felt himself inclined and stirred up in his heart to do this. The men along with (על as in <reference osisRef="Gen.32.12">Gen 32:12</reference>; see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §217) the women brought with a willing heart all kinds of golden rings and jewellery: <hi type="italic">chak</hi>, lit., hook, here a clasp or ring; <hi type="italic">nezem</hi>, an ear or nose-ring (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.4">Gen 35:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.24.47">Gen 24:47</reference>); <hi type="italic">tabbaath</hi>, a finger-ring; <hi type="italic">cumaz</hi>, <hi type="italic">globulus aureus</hi>, probably little golden balls strung together like beads, which were worn by the Israelites and Midianites (Num 31:50) as an ornament round the wrist and neck, as <hi type="italic">Diod. Sic.</hi> relates that they were by the Arabians (3, 44). “<hi type="italic">All kinds of golden jewellery, and every one who had waved</hi> (dedicated) <hi type="italic">a wave</hi> (offering) <hi type="italic">of gold to Jehovah,</hi>” sc., offered it for the work of the tabernacle. The meaning is, that in addition to the many varieties of golden ornaments, which were willingly offered for the work to be performed, every one brought whatever gold he had set apart as a wave-offering (a sacrificial gift) for Jehovah. הניף to <hi type="italic">wave</hi>, lit., to swing or move to and fro, is used in connection with the sacrificial ritual to denote a peculiar ceremony, through which certain portions of a sacrifice, which were not intended for burning upon the altar, but for the maintenance of the priests (Num 18:11), were consecrated to the Lord, or given up to Him in a symbolical manner (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.7.30">Lev 7:30</reference>). <hi type="italic">Tenuphah</hi>, the wave-offering, accordingly denoted primarily those portions of the sacrificial animal which were allotted to the priests as their share of the sacrifices; and then, in a more general sense, every gift or offering that was consecrated to the Lord for the establishment and maintenance of the sanctuary and its worship. In this wider sense the term <hi type="italic">tenuphah</hi> (wave-offering) is applied both here and in <reference osisRef="Exod.38.24">Exo 38:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.38.29">Exo 38:29</reference> to the gold and copper presented by the congregation for the building of the tabernacle. So that it does not really differ from <hi type="italic">terumah</hi>, a <hi type="italic">lift</hi> of heave-offering, as every gift intended for the erection and maintenance of the sanctuary was called, inasmuch as the offerer lifted it off from his own property, to dedicate it to the Lord for the purposes of His worship. Accordingly, in <reference osisRef="Exod.35.24">Exo 35:24</reference> the freewill-offerings of the people in silver and gold for the erection of the tabernacle are called <hi type="italic">terumah</hi>; and in <reference osisRef="Exod.36.6">Exo 36:6</reference>, all the gifts of metal, wood, leather, and woven materials, presented by the people for the erection of the tabernacle, are called קדשׁ תּרוּמת. (On heaving and the heave-offering, see at <reference osisRef="Exod.25.2">Exo 25:2</reference> and Lev 2:9.)
entries.c4b93e9a3c6a9d6009808bb1362eab55dbf329ff: <reference osisRef="Exod.35.25-Exod.35.26">Exo 35:25-26</reference> <div eID="gen1111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1112" type="x-p"/> All the women who understood it (were wise-hearted, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.28.3">Exo 28:3</reference>) spun with their hands, and presented what they spun, viz., the yarn required for the blue and red purple cloth, the crimson and the byssus; from which it is evident that the coloured cloths were dyed in the yarn or in the wool, as was the case in Egypt according to different specimens of old Egyptian cloths (see Hengstenberg, <hi type="italic">Egypt and the Books of Moses</hi>, p. 144). Other women spun goats’ hair for the upper or outer covering of the tent (Exo 26:7.). Spinning was done by the women in very early times (<hi type="italic">Plin. hist. n.</hi> 8, 48), particularly in Egypt, where women are represented on the monuments as busily engaged with the spindle (see Wilkinson, Manners ii. p. 60; iii. p. 133, 136), and at a later period among the Hebrews (<reference osisRef="Prov.31.19">Pro 31:19</reference>). At the present day the women in the peninsula of Sinai spin the materials for their tents from camels’ and goats’ hair, and prepare sheep’s wool for their clothing (<hi type="italic">Rüppell</hi>, <hi type="italic">Nubien</hi>, p. 202); and at Neswa, in the province of <hi type="italic">Omän</hi>, the preparation of cotton yarn is the principal employment of the women (<hi type="italic">Wellstedt</hi>, i. p. 90). Weaving also was, and still is to a great extent, a woman’s work (cf. 2Ki 23:7); it is so among the Arab tribes in the Wady Gharandel, for example (<hi type="italic">Russegger</hi>, iii. 24), and in Nubia (<hi type="italic">Burckhardt</hi>, Nub. p. 211); but at Neswa the weaving is done by the men (<hi type="italic">Wellstedt</hi>). The woven cloths for the tabernacle were prepared by men, partly perhaps because the weaving in Egypt was mostly done by the men (<hi type="italic">Herod</hi>. 2, 35; cf. Hengstenberg, p. 143), but chiefly for this reason, that the cloths for the hangings and curtains were artistic works, which the women did not understand, but which the men had learned in Egypt, where artistic weaving was carried out to a great extent (Wilkinson, iii. pp. 113ff.).<note placement="foot">For drawings of the Egyptian weaving-stool, see Wilkinson, iii. p. 135; also <hi type="italic">Hartmann</hi>, die <hi type="italic">Hebräerinn am Putztisch</hi> i. Taf. 1.</note>
entries.199a822fc39fb5284bc21e1e91ea0908774067b2: <reference osisRef="Exod.35.27-Exod.35.29">Exo 35:27-29</reference> <div eID="gen1112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1113" type="x-p"/> The precious stones for the robes of the high priest, and the spices for the incense and anointing oil, were presented by the princes of the congregation, who had such costly things in their possession.
entries.68d289aa5861dd36d1892238e9a0066f084e30a8: <reference osisRef="Exod.35.30-Exod.35.35">Exo 35:30-35</reference> <div eID="gen1113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1114" type="x-p"/> Moses then informed the people that God had called <hi type="italic">Bezaleel</hi> and <hi type="italic">Aholiab</hi> as master-builders, to complete the building and all the work connected with it, and had not only endowed them with His Spirit, that they might draw the plans for the different works and carry them out, but “had put it into his (Bezaleel’s) heart to teach” (<reference osisRef="Exod.35.34">Exo 35:34</reference>), that is to say, had qualified him to instruct labourers to prepare the different articles under his supervision and guidance. “<hi type="italic">He and Aholiab</hi>” (<reference osisRef="Exod.35.34">Exo 35:34</reference>) are in apposition to “his heart:” into his and Aholiab’s heart (see <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> §121, 3; <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §311 a). The concluding words in <reference osisRef="Exod.35.35">Exo 35:35</reference> are in apposition to אתם (<hi type="italic">them</hi>): “<hi type="italic">them</hi> hath He filled with wisdom...as performers of every kind of work and inventors of designs,” i.e., that they may make every kind of work and may invent designs. In <reference osisRef="Exod.36.1">Exo 36:1</reference>, ועשׂה with <hi type="italic">vav consec</hi>. is dependent upon what precedes, and signifies either, “and so will make,” or, so that he will make (see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §342 b). The idea is this, “Bezaleel, Aholiab, and the other men who understand, into whom Jehovah has infused (בּ נתן) wisdom and understanding, that they may know how to do, shall do every work for the holy service (worship) with regard to (ל as in <reference osisRef="Exod.28.38">Exo 28:38</reference>, etc.) all that Jehovah has commanded.”  <chapter eID="Exod.35"/> <div eID="gen1114" type="x-p"/>

Thus he denominates the artificers, who excelled in shrewdness of intellect, and so, after having commanded them severally of their private means to supply the materials, he now exhorts others to contribute their industry for shaping and joining them together. He then briefly enumerates the parts of the Tabernacle, a longer explanation of which will be seen in chapter 26. This is, therefore, a kind of epitome of all those things, of which he before spoke more in full, since it was necessary to spur them on afresh to the performance of what they had been clearly instructed in. "Particular stress is laid on the contrast, which the condition of the Israelitish nation at that time presents to the splendor and speedy completion of the tent. That tent was certainly splendid, but, in point of fact, exceedingly simple in its construction. If we compare it with the monuments of Egyptian architecture, its relative simplicity must strike us in a much greater degree. As to the materials that were required for it, it admits of proof that the Israelites might well have been possessed of them at that time. The wilderness even might supply them with many of these things. With respect to other things, the metals, precious stones, etc, we must keep in view the condition of a people that had just come out of Egypt. History describes that country as having mercantile transactions with Asia, even from the earliest times. The people had acquired property, in part at least, in Egypt; the description in Exodus 32, leaves us no doubt as to the possessions, and even wealth, that they had gained there. They had not gone out of Egypt empty-handed, but richly provided with silver and gold, 12:36. — “Havernick, Introd. to Pentat. Edin., 1850, pp. 284-285.
how so much wealth could be possessed by a miserably pillaged people, and long driven to servile work; unless it may be inferred from the abundance which is here described, that they were incredibly enriched at their departure from Egypt by the booty which God gave them. The kingdom of Egypt was very wealthy; and its people, as we know, had always been devoted to pleasures and luxuries. What, then, they had accumulated by their rapacity in many years, flowed away from them by the secret influence of God, when they were suddenly made prodigal. But, just as He had blinded the Egyptians, that they should profusely give all they had, so He now directed the minds and hearts of His people, that, mindful of so great a benefit, they should willingly expend, at His command, what they had obtained of His mere grace.

20. And all the congregation of the children of Israel. There is no reason why any one should be surprised that the order of the narrative is changed, since it plainly appears from many passages that the order of time is not always observed by Moses. Thus he appears here to connect the fall of the people with the foregoing injunctions, both with respect to the building of the tabernacle, and the rest of the religious service of God. But I have shewn
See vol. 2, p. 143, and note.
upon good grounds that the tabernacle was built before the people fell into idolatry. Therefore Moses now supplies what had been before omitted, though I have followed the thread of the narrative in order to render it less difficult.
The sum of this relation is, that whatever was necessary for the building of the tabernacle was liberally contributed. It must be observed that they had departed from the presence of Moses: for we gather from this circumstance that, having severally retired to their tents, they had considered apart by themselves what they should give. Hence their liberality is deserving of greater praise, because it was premeditated; for it often happens that when a person has been bountiful from sudden impulse, he afterwards repents of it. When it is added that “they came, every one,” it is a question whether he means that the minds of the whole people were prompt and cheerful in giving, or whether he indirectly rebukes the stinginess and sordidness of those who meanly neglected their duty. In whichever way we choose to take it, Moses repeats what we have seen before, that the offerings were not extorted by force or necessity, but that they proceeded from voluntary and cordial feelings. I thus construe the words, “They came, every one, as his heart stirred each of them up,” as if he had said that they were not compelled by any law imposed upon them, but that every one was his own lawgiver, of his own good-will. This passage is absurdly twisted by the Papists in proof of free-will; as if men were incited by themselves to act rightly and well; for Moses, even while praising their spontaneous feelings, does not mean to exclude the grace of the Spirit, whereby alone our hearts are inclined to holy affections; but this stirring up is contrasted with the unwillingness by which ungodly men are withheld and restrained. Those, therefore, whom the Spirit rules, He does not drag unwillingly by a violent and extrinsic impulse, as it is called, but He so works within them upon their will, that believers stir up themselves, and they voluntarily follow His leadings. So that when it is added, “whose spirit was liberal in himself,”
“Every one, whom his spirit made willing.” — A.V.
the commencement of well-doing is not ascribed to men, nor is even their concurrence praised, as if they co-operated apart from God, but only the internal impulse of their minds, and the sincerity of their desires·
entries.3605b07c4c8d77eb11a17f1188f98511f8ea369f: <div annotateRef="Bible:Exod.35.22" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Exod.35.22" sID="gen17007" type="section"/> <div sID="gen17008" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">22. </hi><hi type="italic">And they came, both men and women</hi>. Express mention is made of the women, not only whose bounty, but whose labors, as it soon afterwards appears, God designed to make use of in the work of the sanctuary. Moses magnifies the fervor of their pious desires, because they did not spare their ornaments; of which people, and especially women, are generally so fond, that they would rather suffer cold, hunger, or thirst, than touch them. <note n="294"> <div sID="gen17009" type="x-p"/> Addition in <hi type="italic">­Fr</hi>., “Pour s’en defaire;” to deprive themselves of them.<div eID="gen17009" type="x-p"/> </note> It was, therefore, a sign of no ordinary zeal to deprive themselves of their rings and bracelets, which many are so slow to part with, even when they are dying of hunger. Again, the contribution of those is praised who gave brass, iron, shittim-wood, and rams’ skins; so that the poor might not doubt but that, although their ability might not be equal to their wishes, the offering, which they presented willingly in their poverty, was no less acceptable to God than when the rich man of his abundance gave what was a hundred times more valuable.<div eID="gen17008" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Exod.35.22" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen17007" osisID="Exod.35.22" type="section"/>

This was a great stimulus to encourage them, when they plainly saw that God presided over the work; a conspicuous proof of which was that new and extraordinary power wherewith Bezaleel and Aboliab were endued; for although they had before been noble and excellent artificers, still there is no doubt but that they were still further endowed with higher gifts, even to a miracle. He again magnifies at greater length the excellence of genius and ability, (which had been given to Bezaleel.) <note n="296"> <div sID="gen17016" type="x-p"/> Added from <hi type="italic">Fr</hi>.<div eID="gen17016" type="x-p"/> </note> For it was a remarkable instance of God’s power, that, after the Israelites had been so contemptuously and oppressively enslaved, there should exist in their nation men still endowed with such talent. God is said to have “filled him with the Spirit of God,” <hi type="italic">i</hi> <hi type="italic">e</hi>., with the Divine Spirit; in order that we may understand that these endowments were not natural to the man, nor even acquired by his own industry. For although even the gifts of nature proceed from the Spirit of God, who gives their intellect to all men no less than their life; still the distribution of peculiar gifts is conspicuous in a higher and different degree. Besides, God had regard to the exquisite nature of this work, so as to endow these artificers with wonderful and extraordinary ability. The faculty of teaching is also added, because two persons by themselves would never have completed so arduous a work in their whole life-time: and this capacity, too, was the gift of Divine grace; <ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="35" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XXXV.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 AND Moses gathered all the congregation of the children of Israel together, and said unto them, These <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> the words which the LORD hath commanded, that ye should do them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 20. 9. Lev. 23. 3. Deut. 5. 12. Luk. 13. 14.</ns0:note> Six days shall work be done, but on the seventh day there shall be to you an <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> Holiness.</ns0:note> holy day, a sabbath of rest to the LORD <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">This command of the sabbath is repeated here, as al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />so <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 31. 13. together with the instructions for the build<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing of the Tabernacle and its utensils, to shew that they were made for no other use than the service of God, which was to be performed as every day, so in an eminent and peculiar man<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ner upon the sabbath day, and to teach them the absolute ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessity of minding that precept in and above all their ceremo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nial observations.</ns0:note>: whosoever doth work therein shall be put to death.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 Ye shall kindle no fire <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">This command seems to be onely temporary and extraor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dinary during the present season and condition, and not extend<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing to succeeding generations. For 1. There are instances of temporary precepts both in the Old and New Testament, which yet are not in their places said to be so. Such were some of the precepts concerning the Passeover. <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 12. 11. as is confessed. And such was<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> that law of abstaining from things strangled and blood, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 15. 2. This precept is nakedly pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />posed, and not called <ns0:hi>a perpetual statute,</ns0:hi> nor enjoyned to be ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />served in their generations, as other precepts are, to whom those or some like clauses are frequently added. 3. The sab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bath is rather a feast-day than a fast-day. And the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> did make feasts and invited guests upon the sabbath-day, which could not probably be without kindling a fire. And, which is more considerable, Christ himself, who fulfilled all righteous<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness and therefore would not have joined in the violation of the sabbath, went to one of those feasts <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 14. And the <ns0:hi>Corinthians</ns0:hi> as they received the Lords Supper upon that day, which none question, so they had their feasts, as is confessed, and apparent from 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11. 21, 22, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> 4. The kindling of a fire was no greater hinderance to the religious observation of the Sabbath than other things which were allowed upon that day, such as the washing and dressing of themselves, eating and drinking, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> 5. This prohibition doth not seem to concern the dressing of meat, as many understand it by comparing this with <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 16. 23. (which place I humbly conceive is misun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstood, as I have there intimated, for that was lawful to be done upon their most solemn days, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 12. 16.) but the service of the Tabernacle, which is the subject of this chapter and the occasion of these words, and the sence seems to be this, You shall kindle no fire for any handy-work throughout your habitation, no not for the service of this Tabernacle, for the heating of any tools, or the melting of any metals, or other things belonging to it, which being to be made for Gods ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vice, and deserving and requiring all expedition, they might probably conceive that such work might be done upon that <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>y. And here also, as oft elsewhere, under one kind all the rest are comprehended and forbidden.</ns0:note> throughout your habitations upon the sabbath day.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 And Moses spake unto all the congregation of the children of Israel, saying, This <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the thing which the LORD commanded, saying,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 Take ye from amongst you an offering unto the LORD: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 25. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> whosoever <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> of a willing heart <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">For God values not forced or grudged services, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 9. 7.</ns0:note>, let him bring it, an offering of the LORD, gold, and silver, and brass,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And blue, and purple, and scarlet, and fine linnen, and goats <ns0:hi>hair.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And rams skins died red, and badgers skins, and shittim-wood,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 And oil for the light, and spices for anoint<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing oil, and for the sweet incense:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 And onyx stones, and stones to be set for the ephod, and for the breast-plate.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 31. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> every wise-hearted <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Skilful artist: for though God had prescribed the things yet it required Wisdom and skill to execute what God commanded.</ns0:note> among you, shall come, and make all that the LORD hath commanded.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">ch. 26. 1, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> The tabernacle <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) The boards or structure of the Tabernacle, as it ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pears because it is distinguished here from its tent and curtains, whereas elsewhere, the <ns0:hi>Tabernacle</ns0:hi> is put for all together.</ns0:note>, his tent <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The inward and finer curtains which covered the boards of it.</ns0:note>, and his covering <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The outward and courser coverings.</ns0:note>, his taches, and his boards, his bars, his pillars, and his sockets:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 The ark, and the staves thereof, <ns0:hi>with</ns0:hi> the mercy-seat, and the vail of the covering <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Which was hanged before the Ark and Mercy<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />seat.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 The table, and his staves, and all his vessels, and the shew-bread <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">But neither did God prescribe the making of the shew<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bread amongst the other utensils, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 25. nor was this made by the workmen here spoken of, but by others. How then comes this to be mentioned here? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> 1. <ns0:hi>The shew-bread</ns0:hi> may be here put for the vessels for the receiving of the shew-bread, by an usual Metonymy of the adjunct, the thing contained put for the thing containing, as <ns0:hi>treasures</ns0:hi> are put for the place where the treasures are put, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 135. 7. <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 2. 11. and 12. 35. and <ns0:hi>the gifts</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>offerings of God</ns0:hi> for the treasury where they were put, <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 21. 4. Hence <ns0:hi>Tremellius</ns0:hi> renders this place, <ns0:hi>and the</ns0:hi> vessels of <ns0:hi>the shew-bread.</ns0:hi> Obj. <ns0:hi>All the vessels</ns0:hi> of the Table are mentioned before, of which this was one. <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> It is not un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />usual after a general expression comprehending all distinctly to name one eminent member of that kind, such as this un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />questionably was, the table being made principally for this use. Thus <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 16. 7. <ns0:hi>Tell my disciples and Peter.</ns0:hi> Like examples are in 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 2. 30. 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 11. 1. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 18. the Title. <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 1. 14. and in other Authors. And for the particle <ns0:hi>Vau, and,</ns0:hi> which may seem to imply that these were things of another kind, and not any vessels of the Table, that is oft put for <ns0:hi>espe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cially,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 2. 1. <ns0:hi>Mark.</ns0:hi> 16. 7. and so onely notes an emi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nent thing of the same kind, as hath been said. <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> 2. Though God did not prescribe the making of the shew-bread, yet he mentions it, together with the table, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 25. 30. and there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore it is conveniently mentioned with the table in this place also, where <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> to shew his exactness and fidelity, doth pun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctually repeat the same things to the people which he had re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceived in command from God. In like manner the oil, which fed the light of the lamps, is mentioned here in the next verse, because the <ns0:hi>lighting of the lamps</ns0:hi> was prescribed, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 25. 37.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="34">34 And he hath put in his heart, that he may teach <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">To wit, others to work under him: for the work required many hands: and it is a peculiar gift of God to be apt to teach, which every skilful man hath not.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>both</ns0:hi> he, and Aholiab the son of Ahisa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mach of the tribe of Dan.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="35">35 Them hath he filled with wisdom of heart, to work all manner of work of the ingraver, and of the cunning workman, and of the embroider<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />er, in blue, and in purple, in scarlet, and in fine linen, and of the weaver, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> of them that do any work, and of those that devise cunning work.</ns0:p>
